section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains how Cortes's few hundred men were able to carry out the actions described in the passage?

stimulus.text:

"In these chapels are the images or idols... the principal ones, in which the people have greatest faith and confidence, I precipitated from their pedestals, and cast them down the steps of the temple, purifying the chapels in which they had stood, as they were all polluted with human blood, shed in the sacrifices. In the places of these I put images of our Lady and the Saints... items.stem: Logan's speech best illustrates which of the following?

stimulus.text:

"I appeal to any white man to say if ever he entered Logan's cabin hungry and he gave him not meat... During the course of the last long and bloody war Logan remained idle in his cabin, an advocate for peace... I had even thought to have lived with you but for the injuries of one man. Colonel Cresap, the last spring, in cold blood and unprovoked, murdered all the relations of Logan... There runs not a drop of my blood in the veins of any living creature. items.stem: In what way did the actions of Abraham Lincoln in 1860 contradict Douglass’s sentiments in the excerpt above?

stimulus.text: “In one view the slaveholders have a decided advantage over all opposition. It is well to notice this advantage—the advantage of complete organization. They are organized; and yet were not at the pains of creating their organizations. The State governments, where the system of slavery exists, are complete slavery organizations. The church organizations in those States are equally at the service of slavery; while the Federal Government, with its army and navy, from the chief magistracy in Washington, to the Supreme Court, and thence to the chief marshalship at New York, is pledged to support, defend, and propagate the crying curse of human bondage. The pen, the purse, and the sword, are united against the simple truth, preached by humble men in obscure places.” Source: Frederick Douglass, “The Dred Scott Decision” (speech), 1857 (public domain).

options: Lincoln promoted the freedom of settlers within territories to determine the slave status of their new state.

items.stem: The audience for Roosevelt’s speech likely would have been most supportive of which of the following policies of the Roosevelt administration?

stimulus.text: “It is not enough to be well-meaning and kindly, but weak; neither is it enough to be strong, unless morality and decency go hand in hand with strength. We must possess the qualities which make us do our duty in our homes and among our neighbors, and in addition we must possess the qualities which are indispensable to the make-up of every great and masterful nation—the qualities of courage and hardihood, of individual initiative and yet of power to combine for a common end, and above all, the resolute determination to permit no man and no set of men to sunder us one from the other by lines of caste or creed or section. We must act upon the motto of all for each and each for all. There must be ever present in our minds the fundamental truth that in a republic such as ours the only safety is to stand neither for nor against any man because he is rich or because he is poor, because he is engaged in one occupation or another, because he works with his brains or because he works with his hands. We must treat each man on his worth and merits as a man. We must see that each is given a square deal, because he is entitled to no more and should receive no less.” Source: Theodore Roosevelt, a speech to farmers in New York, 1903

section_1b.directions: Section I, Part B — Short Answer: 3 questions, 40 minutes. Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (A, B, C); write your answers in complete sentences. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, Question 2 on a primary source, and Question 3 on a non-text source (map, chart, image, or diagram). This part counts for 20 percent of the exam score.

questions.stimulus_text: Historian Edmund Morgan argues that the French and Indian War transformed the imperial relationship: 'The removal of the French menace deprived the colonists of their chief reason for depending on the mother country, while the cost of the war gave the mother country its chief reason for taxing them.'
parts: A. Briefly explain ONE reason for conflict between the colonies and the British government in the 1760s and 1770s.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND reason for that conflict.
C. Briefly explain ONE way colonists expressed opposition to British actions.
exemplar: Victory in the French and Indian War removed France as a serious military threat in North America, so the colonists no longer needed British troops for their security and resented paying for them.
The war left Britain with a massive debt, and Parliament tried to make the colonies pay through measures like the Stamp Act and Townshend duties — Parliament's first direct taxes on the colonists.

Colonists expressed opposition through boycotts of British goods, the Stamp Act Congress, committees of correspondence, and ultimately the First Continental Congress, which organized colonial resistance.

questions.stimulus_text:
"For the purposes hereinbefore set forth the Secretary shall cause to be made, by inspectors appointed for that purpose, an examination and inspection of all cattle, sheep, swine, and goats before they shall be allowed to enter into any slaughtering, packing, or canning establishment..."
—Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906 (abridged)
parts: A. Briefly explain ONE example of Progressive action to reform the American economy.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND example of Progressive economic reform.
C. Briefly explain ONE example of Progressive action to reform American politics.
exemplar: Reform mayors like Cleveland's Tom Johnson municipalized utilities to give citizens cheaper, better service, while governors like Wisconsin's La Follette regulated railroads and pushed direct primaries.
At the federal level, Roosevelt's trust-busting and the Hepburn Act (1906) strengthened railroad regulation, and the Pure Food and Drug and Meat Inspection Acts protected consumers.
Politically, Progressives pushed direct democracy: the initiative, referendum, recall, direct election of senators (Seventeenth Amendment), and women's suffrage (Nineteenth Amendment).

questions.stimulus_text: The diagram shows the triangular trade of the 1700s. One arrow runs from New England to West Africa labeled 'rum and manufactured goods.' A second arrow runs from West Africa to the West Indies labeled 'enslaved Africans (Middle Passage).' A third arrow runs from the West Indies back to New England labeled 'sugar and molasses.'
parts: A. Identify and briefly explain ONE pattern shown in the triangular trade diagram.
B. Briefly explain ONE way the British imperial system affected the colonies.
C. Briefly explain ONE way the colonies resisted greater British control.
exemplar: The diagram shows a three-legged circuit: New England ships carried rum to Africa, traded it for enslaved people, and returned with sugar and molasses from the West Indies. The pattern reveals how deeply the northern colonial economy depended on slavery even where plantations were rare.

One way the imperial system affected the colonies was through the Navigation Acts of 1660 and 1663, which forced colonists to ship tobacco, rice, and sugar to England and to route European goods through English ports, enriching English merchants at colonial expense.

Colonists resisted tighter control by smuggling and by defying royal authority — Massachusetts's defiance of the Navigation Acts helped provoke the Dominion of New England, and colonial assemblies used their 'power of the purse' to frustrate royal governors.

section_2a.directions: Section II, Part A — Document-Based Question: 1 question, 60 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period). The question is based on 7 documents. In your response you must develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, use at least 4 documents to support your argument, use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents, and for at least 2 documents explain how the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to your argument. This part counts for 25 percent of the exam score.

dbq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which fears of communism affected American society from 1940 to 1959.

documents.text: Paraphrased from a decoded telegram from a KGB agent in New York to Moscow, intercepted by U.S. intelligence. The agent reports that LIBERAL (identified in the notes as Julius Rosenberg) has successfully recruited Kh'YuS (probably Joel Barr or Alfred Sarant), that the two will be given a camera to photograph their own materials, and that OSA (Ruth Greenglass) has agreed to help draw in ShMEL' (David Greenglass) with a view to ENORMOUS (the atomic energy project).
documents.sourcing_note: POV: Soviet intelligence operative. Purpose: operational report to headquarters. Audience: Moscow (Lt. Gen. P. M. Fitin). Argument relevance: evidence that Soviet espionage in the United States was real - grounding some anti-communist fears in fact.

documents.text: Paraphrased from Representative John F. Kennedy, speech to Congress. Kennedy declares that the United States has suffered a disaster in China, blames the administration for failing to prevent the communist victory there, and demands stronger American action against communism in Asia.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: ambitious Cold Warrior congressman. Purpose: attack the Truman administration and demand a harder anti-communist line. Audience: House and the public. Argument relevance: shows anti-communism as a domestic political weapon - 'losing China' became a partisan charge.

documents.text: Paraphrased from President Harry Truman, speech. Truman recounts that Americans had become so frightened of being called communists that some were afraid to sign their names to quotations from the Declaration of Independence, and warns that the nation must not let fear destroy the very freedoms it claims to defend.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: sitting president. Purpose: decry the excesses of the anti-communist scare while defending his own anti-communism. Audience: the public. Argument relevance: illustrates the climate of fear at its height - and Truman's dual role as both Cold Warrior and critic of the witch hunt.

documents.text: A still from the Federal Civil Defense Administration's 1951 instructional film Duck and Cover, produced for schoolchildren: the film taught children to shield themselves under desks ('duck and cover') during an atomic-bomb drill.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: federal civil-defense agency. Purpose: prepare schoolchildren for atomic attack. Audience: schoolchildren and teachers. Argument relevance: shows the state embedding H-bomb fear in children's daily routines - the scare reached the classroom.
documents.caption: Still from the Federal Civil Defense Administration's 1951 instructional film Duck and Cover, teaching schoolchildren the 'duck and cover' atomic-bomb drill
documents.pd_rationale: 1951; U.S. federal work: still from the Federal Civil Defense Administration film 'Duck and Cover'; license PD-USGov on Commons (verified in file-page wikitext)

documents.text: Described from 'The Red Round-Up,' a Clifford K. Berryman cartoon in the Washington Evening Star (November 8, 1919), drawn the day after the Palmer Raids began: Uncle Sam holds a large net full of scruffy arrested men, saying 'Now to put 'em where they cant do anymore harm.'
documents.sourcing_note: POV: mainstream press cartoonist. Purpose: cheer the Palmer Raids roundup of suspected radicals. Audience: newspaper readers. Argument relevance: First Red Scare imagery the Second Red Scare echoed - federal power sweeping up 'dangerous' foreigners.
documents.caption: 'The Red Round-Up': Clifford K. Berryman cartoon, Washington Evening Star, November 8, 1919 - Uncle Sam holds a net full of arrested radicals: 'Now to put 'em where they cant do anymore harm'
documents.pd_rationale: Published 1919-11-08 in the Washington Evening Star (source: Chronicling America, Library of Congress); license PD-US on Commons (pre-1930 U.S. publication; verified in file-page wikitext)

documents.text: Paraphrased from Senator Joseph McCarthy, speech at Wheeling, West Virginia. McCarthy claims to hold a list of 205 communists working in the State Department, accusing the government of harboring traitors shaping American foreign policy.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: demagogic senator. Purpose: gain national attention and political power. Audience: a Republican women's club, via the press. Argument relevance: the epitome of reckless accusation driving the scare - the charge that launched McCarthyism.

documents.text: Paraphrased from Edward R. Murrow, television broadcast. Murrow warns that McCarthy confuses dissent with disloyalty, that accusation is not proof, and that the senator's methods threaten the freedoms Americans claim to defend against communism.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: respected broadcast journalist. Purpose: check McCarthy's power. Audience: television viewers. Argument relevance: turning point - establishment media pushback that helped end McCarthy's influence, showing the scare's limits.

section_2b.directions: Section II, Part B — Long Essay: 1 question, 40 minutes. Develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, and support your argument with specific and relevant examples. This part counts for 15 percent of the exam score. Total exam time: 3 hours 15 minutes.

leq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which late nineteenth century urbanization affected politics, immigration, and popular culture.
leq.guidance: Thesis frame: argue how rapid city growth reorganized American life. Evidence buckets: machine politics and municipal reform; new immigration and ethnic neighborhoods; mass culture (vaudeville, sports, department stores); Progressive responses to urban problems.
